# Deriving Canonical Gradients

In the previous chapter we discovered that every pathwise-differentiable estimand has at least one RAL estimator and that any asymptotically optimal RAL estimator has an influence function equal to the canonical gradient (the *efficient* influence function; EIF). In the next part of the book we'll tackle the problem of constructing estimators that have this property, but, in order to do that we need to know what the canonical gradient is for any estimand and model of interest. In this chapter we'll therefore learn techniques to derive the canonical gradient.

There are many methods to derive canonical gradients that are more or less natural to depending on the kind of model and estimand. In this book we'll first focus on point mass contamination: a simple technique that works well in locally nonparametric models. In the process of illustrating this technique we'll cover some handy rules that make it easier to build canonical gradients up out of simpler blocks. Then we will discuss projection methods which are often useful when the model is restricted in some way and in particular for models where some factors of the joint distribution are known.

## Point Mass Contamination

Point mass contamination (also referred to as the "Gateaux derivative" or "Hampel influence function" approach) is a easy-to-use strategy for deriving the gradient in nonparametric models (recall there is only one gradient in a nonparametric model). Nonparametric models are a good starting point because often we don't know anything useful about the data-generating distribution. Even if we do, nonparametric models are a reasonable fallback because we can still produce a good RAL estimator using the nonparametric EIF - it will just be less efficient than the efficient estimator under the restricted model that exploits our prior knowledge. We will also see in a few sections that knowing the nonparametric canonical gradient is useful when deriving the canonical gradient in restricted models.

The idea of point mass contamination is to find paths in directions that make it easy to compute the value of the gradient at a given point $z$. We'll see that it suffices to take convex paths in the direction of distribution that is a point mass at a point $z$.

### Discrete Distributions

Presume for a moment that we're working in a model where every variable is discrete but otherwise unspecified. When this is the case, the model is actually parametric because any joint distribution is a categorical distribution over a finite number of support points. Another way of putting this is that in a dataset drawn from such a distribution, there are only a finite number of possible "rows" that can appear. The probability distribution assigns a probability $\p\{Z=z_j\} = \p_j$ to each unique row $z_j$ in a discrete set $\mathcal Z$: the probabilities $p_j$ for $j \in \{1\dots J\}$ are the only parameters.

Let's say we're at a point $p$ (representing either the mass function or the vector of probabilities, they are essentially the same). We can construct a convex path in the parameter space with $p$ as the starting point and as the endpoint the mass function $1^* = 1(z=z^*)$ (with distribution $\mathbb 1^*$) that puts all the probability mass at some point $z^* \in \{z_1 \dots z_J\}$. For small values of $\eps$, the convex path

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_\eps 
&= (1-\eps)p + \eps 1^*  \\
&= p + \eps (1^*- p)
\end{aligned}
$$

represents the distribution $p$ "contaminated" with a little bit of extra mass at the point $z^*$. Clearly all elements of the path are within the model. Moreover, this path is differentiable. Assuming none of the components of $p$ (as a vector) are zero, the score for such a path (see @exm-convex-path-score) is

$$
s^* = \left(\frac{1^*}{p} - 1 \right)
.
$$

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-discrete-model-local-nonparam}
When $\p$ is a discrete distribution over a set of $J$ points $\mathcal Z = \{z_1 \dots z_J\}$ with mass function $p$, the space $\eltwop$ is all functions $f$ such that $\E_\p[f(Z)^2] = \sum_j^J f(z_j)^2\ p(z_j)$ is finite (and two functions are considered "equivalent" if they agree on the points $\mathcal Z$).

Prove that the discrete model $\model$ consisting of all distributions $\p$ supported on the same set $\mathcal Z$ is locally nonparametric (@def-nonparam-model) at any point, despite being a parametric model with $J$ parameters!
:::
::::

Consider now the inner product $\p_\theta s^* \grad\Psi$ where $\grad\Psi$ is taken to be the (unknown) gradient at $\p$. Since the distributions in question are discrete, the expected value of any function $f$ is $\p f = \sum_{z \in \mathcal Z} f(z) p(z)$. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\p s^* \grad\Psi 
&= \p \frac{1^*}{p} \grad\Psi - \underbrace{\p \grad\Psi}_0 \\
&= \sum_z \frac{1^*(z)}{p(z)} \grad\Psi(z) p(z) \\
&= \grad\Psi(z^*).
\end{aligned}
$$

For intuition, recall that one way to think of a function is as a very long "vector" $\grad\Psi = [\dots \grad\Psi(0.1), \dots \grad\Psi(3.4) \dots]$ where the elements correspond to different possible values of the argument (see @sec-app-L2-vectors). The scores above look like $1(z=z^*)$ so when we take an inner product of such a score with an arbitrary function, we essentially pick out the element of that function corresponding to position $z^*$. In other words, the directions corresponding to point masses at each $z^*$ are like the "axes" of the space and we get the value of our unknown function at each point by projecting onto those axes.

Knowing that $\p s^* \grad\Psi = \grad\Psi(z^*)$ isn't immediately helpful because we still have the unknown gradient on both sides of the equation. But by the central identity of influence functions we can now replace the inner product with the pathwise derivative $\dot\Psi(s^*) = \p s^* \grad\Psi = \grad\Psi(z^*)$.

Read right-to-left, this gives us a way of deriving the gradient $\grad\Psi$, which we don't know. All we need to do to obtain the values of $\grad\Psi$ at each point $z^*$ is compute the pathwise derivative along convex paths in the direction of each point mass $1^*$. Specifically, we must evaluate

$$
\dot\Psi(s^*)
= \ddeps \Psi\bigg(\p + \eps (\mathbb 1^* - \p) \bigg)
.
$$

::: {.Exm #exm-point-mass-mean-EIF}
# Gradient of mean

Let $Z$ be a one-dimensional discrete random variable with no other restrictions and let $\Psi(\p) = \E_\p[Z]$, the population mean. By the above,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\grad\Psi(z^*) 
&= \ddeps \Psi\bigg(\p + \eps (\mathbb 1^* - \p) \bigg) \\
&= \ddeps \sum_z z \bigg( p(z) + \eps (1^*(z)- p(z)) \bigg) \\
&= \sum_k z 1^*(z) - \sum_z z p(z) \\
&= z^* - \E_{\p}[Z]
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $\grad\Psi(z) =  z - \E_\p[Z]$, which is the influence function for the sample mean and aligns with the equivalent result we proved in @exm-gradient-nonparam.
:::

Keep in mind that the gradient $\grad\Psi$ depends on the data-generating distribution (and the model but here we have a fixed discrete model in mind), so really we should be writing $\grad_\p \Psi$. In @exm-point-mass-mean-EIF this is evident because the result depends on $\E_\p[Z]$.

The manipulations in @exm-point-mass-mean-EIF are characteristic of gradient derivations with point mass contamination. The only challenge is keeping careful track of the point mass $z^*$ vs generic values $z$ and the action of the indicator functions. This is a purely mechanical exercise, no special intuition is requred. Just keep in mind that $\sum_z f(z)\  1^*(z) = f(z^*)$ because the indicator "picks out" the indicated term in the sum. Once you've done it once or twice it becomes straightforward.

Sometimes you also need to keep track of some other fixed point, as the next example shows.

::: {.Exm #exm-point-mass-density}
# Gradient of a density at a point

Let $Z$ be a one-dimensional discrete random variable with no other restrictions and let $\Psi(\p) = \p \{ Z= \tilde z \}$ for a particular value $\tilde z$.

An easy way to derive the canonical gradient is to let $W = 1(Z= \tilde z)$ and use the result from @exm-point-mass-mean-EIF since $\p\{Z= \tilde z\} = \E_\p[W]$. This immediately gives $\grad\Psi(z) =  1_{\tilde z}(z) - p(\tilde z)$.

We arrive at the same result if we consider that $\Psi(\p) =  p(\tilde z)$. For any $\tilde z$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\grad\Psi(z^*) &= \ddeps \Psi\bigg(\p + \eps (\mathbb 1^* - \p) \bigg) \\
&= \ddeps \bigg[\big(p + \eps ( 1^* - p) \big)(\tilde z)\bigg] \\
&= 1^*(\tilde z) - p(\tilde z)
.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the same as above because $1^*(\tilde z) = 1(z^* = \tilde z) = 1_{\tilde z}(z^*)$.
:::

When $Z$ is multidimensional the same process works but the notation can be more verbose. For example, if $Z = (Y,X)$, then the $Z$-domain $\mathcal Z = \{z_1, \dots z_J\}$ is some subset of the cartesian product $\mathcal Y \times \mathcal X$ where these are the (discrete) domains of $X$ and $Y$. We'll let $z^* = (y^*, x^*)$ be the point at which mass is concentrated in the mass function $1^*$ with corresponding distribution $\mathbb 1^*$. In an abuse of notation we'll also write, e.g., $1^*(x) = 1(x=x^*)$. This single-variable indicator also picks out terms in a sum, i.e., $\sum_{x,y} f(x,y) 1^*(x) = \sum_y f(x^*, y)$. We'll see patterns like this a lot in gradient derivations using point mass contamination.

::: {.Exm #exm-point-mass-cond-mean-EIF}
# Gradient of a conditional mean

Let $(Y,X)$ be discrete random variables with no other restrictions and let $\Psi(\p) = \E_\p[Y|X=\tilde x]$, the conditional mean of $Y$ at a value $X=\tilde x$. Computing the pathwise derivative on a path from a distribution $p$ towards a point mass at $(y^*, x^*)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\grad\Psi(y^*,x^*) 
&= \ddeps \Psi\bigg( p + \eps (1^* - p) \bigg) \\
&= \ddeps \sum_y y \bigg( p + \eps (1^*- p) \bigg)(y|\tilde x) \\
&= \sum_y y \ddeps \bigg( p + \eps (1^*- p) \bigg)(y|\tilde x) \\
\end{aligned}
$$

The densities can only be summed as joint densities so to compute the conditional density above we must do some algebra. Applying the identity $p(y|x) = \frac{p(y,x)}{p(x)} = \frac{p(y,x)}{\sum_y p(y,x)}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bigg( p + \eps (1^*- p) \bigg)(y|\tilde x)
&=  \frac{\big( p + \eps (1^*- p) \big)(y,\tilde x)} { \sum_y \big( p + \eps (1^*- p) \big)(y, \tilde x)} \\
&=  \frac{p(y, \tilde x) + \eps (1^*(y, \tilde x)- p(y, \tilde x))} 
    { \sum_y p(y, \tilde x) + \sum_y \eps (1^*(y, \tilde x) - p(y, \tilde x))} \\
&=  \frac{p(y, \tilde x) + \eps (1^*(y, \tilde x)- p(y, \tilde x))} 
    { p(\tilde x) + \eps (1^*(\tilde x) - p(\tilde x))} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Now we plug this into to the display above and use $\ddeps \frac{a + b\eps}{c + d\eps} = \frac{b}{c} - \frac{ad}{c^2}$ (by the chain and quotient rules) to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\grad\Psi(y^*, x^*)
&= \sum_y y \ddeps \left(
    \frac{p(y, \tilde x) + \eps (1^*(y, \tilde x)- p(y, \tilde x))} 
    { p(\tilde x) + \eps (1^*(\tilde x) - p(\tilde x))} 
  \right)\\
&= \sum_y y
    \left(\frac{1^*(y, \tilde x)- p(y, \tilde x)}{p(\tilde x)} -  
    \frac{(1^*(\tilde x) - p(\tilde x))p(y, \tilde x)}{p(\tilde x)^2}
    \right)
    \\
&= \frac{1}{p(\tilde x)} \sum_y y     
    \bigg(1^*(y, \tilde x)- p(y, \tilde x) -  
    (1^*(\tilde x) - p(\tilde x))p(y| \tilde x)
    \bigg)
    \\
&= \frac{1}{p(\tilde x)} \sum y {1^*(y,\tilde x) - 1^*(\tilde x)p(y|\tilde x)}
\\
&= \frac{1^*(\tilde x)}{p(\tilde x)}\left(y^* - \E[Y|X=\tilde x] \right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $\grad\Psi(y,x) = \frac{1(x=\tilde x)}{p(\tilde x)}\left(y - \E[Y|X=\tilde x] \right)$. The conditional mean is generally not pathwise differentiable and thus doesn't have an gradient (see @exm-unbounded-estimand), but in discrete data models it is!
:::

As in the one-dimensional model, the difficulty in these calculations is keeping track of what is the fixed point $\tilde x$, what is the location of the point mass $(y^* ,x^*)$, and what is a generic value $(y,x)$. Go slowly and deliberately at first and you will get the hang of it.

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-point-mass-conditional-density}
# Gradient of a conditional density

Let $(Y,X)$ be discrete random variables with no other restrictions and let $\Psi(\p) = \p \{ Y=\tilde y | X = \tilde x \}$ for particular values $\tilde y, \tilde x$. What is the canonical gradient for this estimand at a point $\p$ in this model?

*Hint: let* $W = 1(Y=\tilde y)$ and use the result from @exm-point-mass-mean-EIF since $\p\{Y=\tilde y|X=\tilde x\} = \E_\p[W|X=\tilde x]$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-gradient-cov}
# Gradient of the covariance

Let $(Y,X)$ be discrete random variables with no other restrictions and let $\Psi(\p) = \C_\p [ Y,X ]$. What is the canonical gradient for this estimand at a point $\p$ in this model?
:::
::::

### General Distributions

Point mass contamination is easiest to present for discrete models but it also works for general nonparametric models. However, it's more difficult to understand in the general setting because "point masses" don't exist for continuous random variables. Nonetheless, in much of the literature you'll see point masses in continuous densities represented informally using Dirac delta functions. @hines-eif has many good examples.

The derivation with Dirac deltas can be made rigorous (see @ichimura2022influence), but, following the advice of @kennedy-review, I find it much easier to simply pretend the model is discrete! Perhaps surprisingly, the form of the gradient in an unrestricted discrete model is generally also the form of the gradient in the nonparametric model. If you are worried, it is easy to check that the result holds by verifying the central identify for influence functions, since in a nonparametric model there is only one function (the gradient) for which it will hold.

::: {.Exm #exm-point-mass-mean-check}
In @exm-point-mass-mean-EIF we showed that, in discrete data models, the gradient for the mean is $\grad\Psi(z) =  z - \E_\p[Z]$. We now verify that this is also the gradient in the nonparametric model by checking that $\dot\Psi_\p(s) = \p s \grad\Psi$ for all $s \in \eltwopz$.

In @exm-gradient-nonparam we already derived that $\dot\Psi_\p(s) = \E[Zs(Z)]$ for the mean. On the other hand,

$$
\p s\grad\Psi = \E [s(Z)(Z - \E[Z])] = \E [s(Z)Z] - \E[Z] \underbrace{\E[s(Z)]}_0
,
$$

which establishes the desired equality.
:::

Of course, we already knew the gradient for the mean in the nonparametric model since we derived it in @exm-gradient-nonparam. But in that proof we had to magically know to add "zero" to the inner product in order to get a zero mean score. In practice, such tricks are not readily apparent. It's much easier to have a candidate gradient and simply check that it works, as we just did in @exm-point-mass-mean-check.

Some estimands, however, are pathwise differentiable in discrete models but not in nonparametric models. When this happens you will see a specific kind of failure when you check $\dot\Psi_\p(s) = \p s \grad\Psi$ for all $s \in \eltwopz$.

::: {.Exm #exm-point-mass-cond-mean-check}
In @exm-point-mass-mean-EIF we showed that, in discrete data models, the gradient for the conditional mean of $Y$ at a point $X=\tilde x$ is $\grad\Psi(y,x) = \frac{1(x=\tilde x)}{p(\tilde x)}\left(y - \E[Y|X=\tilde x] \right)$. We now show that it is *not* the gradient in a nonparametric model. In fact, there is no gradient in a nonparametric model because this estimand is not pathwise differentiable in such models.

Assuming we did not know about the lack of pathwise differentiability, we might try to check $\dot\Psi_\p(s) = \p s \grad\Psi$. On the right-hand side, for any distribution where $Y$ and $X$ are continuously-distributed with density $p(y,x)$

$$
\p s\grad\Psi = \int s(y,x)\frac{1(x=\tilde x)}{p(\tilde x)}\left(y - \E[Y|X=\tilde x] \right) p(y,x) \dd (y,x)
$$

which is always zero if $1(x=\tilde x)$ is interpreted as a standard indicator function. This doesn't make sense because it implies that the pathwise derivative is zero everywhere, meaning that the estimand is constant across the model, which it certainly isn't.

Things make a little more sense if you interpret the indicator as a Dirac delta instead. In @hines-eif, the equivalent derivation of the gradient using Dirac delta functions produces

$$
\grad\Psi(y,x) = \frac{\infty(x=\tilde x)}{p(x)}\left(y - \E[Y|X=\tilde x] \right)
$$

where $\infty(x=\tilde x)$ is the Dirac delta that returns $\infty$ at $x=\tilde x$ and zero elsewhere and which magically picks values out of integrals, i.e., $\int \infty(x=\tilde x) f(x) \dd x = f(\tilde x)$.

However, we know that any gradient must be in $\eltwopz$, i.e. it must be square-integrable. But this function is not:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\| \grad\Psi \|^2
&= \int \grad\Psi(y,x)^2\  p(y,x) \dd(y,x) \\
&= \int \frac{\infty(x=\tilde x)^2}{p(x)^2}\left(y - \E[Y|X=\tilde x] \right)^2 \ p(y,x)\dd(y,x)  \\
&= \int \infty(x=\tilde x) \frac{\infty(x=\tilde x)}{p(x)} {\left( \int \left(y - \E[Y|X=\tilde x] \right)^2 \ p(y|x)\dd y \right)} \dd x  \\
&= \frac{\infty(\tilde x = \tilde x)}{p(\tilde x)} \V[Y|X=\tilde x] = \infty
\\
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

The failures shown in @exm-point-mass-cond-mean-check above are typical of what happens when you use point mass contamination to try and derive the gradient for an estimand that is not nonparametrically pathwise differentiable. If you end up with an indicator of a possibly continuous value in the gradient, it's a good sign that the estimand is not nonparametrically pathwise differentiable.

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-point-mass-density-nonparam}
Show that the gradient we derived for $\Psi(\p) = \p \{ Z=\tilde z \}$ in @exm-point-mass-density breaks down if it is treated as the gradient in a nonparametric model.
:::
::::

Although appealing to a discrete data model usually does the trick, there are times when it doesn't work. This can happen for estimands that are defined implicitly rather than explicitly in terms of expectations or probabilities. The point-mass contamination strategy is still useful, but we need a different approach to evaluate the pathwise derivative. I give an example here to demonstrate this, but it's not vitally important to understand in detail.

:::: {.Exm #exm-quantile-gradient}
# Gradient of a quantile

Let $\mathcal P$ be all continuous distributions $\p$ of a single variable $Z$ and let the estimand $\Psi(\p)$ be the $q$th quantile of $Z$ under $\p$. Our aim is to find the canonical gradient of $\Psi$ in this model.

Abusing notation a bit, let $\p(z)$ denote the CDF of $Z$ under $\p$. The quantile $\psi$ is defined by $\p(\psi) = q$ so we can write $\Psi(\p) = \p^{-1}(q)$ since the inverse of the CDF of a continuous random variable is well-defined, or

$$
\Psi(\p) = \inf \{ z: \p(z) \ge q\}
$$

for general distributions.

Along the convex path $\p^{(\eps)} = \p + \eps(\mathbb 1^* - \p)$, the CDF is

$$
[\p + \eps(\mathbb 1^* - \p)](z) = \p(z) + \eps(\mathbb 1^*(z) - \p(z))
$$

where $\mathbb 1^*(z) = 1(z \ge z^*)$ is the CDF of a point mass at $z^*$.

Technically this is not a legitimate path because $\mathbb 1^* \not\in \mathcal P$ and in fact the path is not differentiable, but we can interpret it as the limit of a sequence of differentiable paths. @ichimura2022influence has the details but we don't need to make a fully-rigorous argument: as with assuming a discrete model in other problems, using this path is just a tool to come up with a candidate gradient.

::: {#fig-quantile-gradient}
``` tikz
\pgfplotsset{compat=1.18}

% Logistic CDF and logit
\pgfmathdeclarefunction{Logistic}{1}{\pgfmathparse{1/(1 + exp(-#1))}}
\pgfmathdeclarefunction{logit}{1}{\pgfmathparse{ln(#1/(1-#1))}}

% ===== Parameters =====
\def\q{0.55}        % quantile level
\def\eps{0.3}       % mixture weight
\def\zstep{-0.5}    % location of the point mass
% =======================

% Precompute thresholds
\pgfmathsetmacro{\Fzstar}{Logistic(\zstep-1)}
\pgfmathsetmacro{\Fleft}{(1-\eps)*\Fzstar}
\pgfmathsetmacro{\Fright}{\Fleft+\eps}

% Compute psi_eps depending on where q falls
\pgfmathsetmacro{\xpsiBefore}{1 + logit(\q/(1-\eps))}
\pgfmathsetmacro{\xpsiAfter}{1 + logit((\q-\eps)/(1-\eps))}
\pgfmathsetmacro{\xpsi}{
  (\q < \Fleft)    * \xpsiBefore +
  (\q >= \Fleft && \q <= \Fright) * \zstep +
  (\q > \Fright)   * \xpsiAfter
}

% Logistic-only quantile
\pgfmathsetmacro{\xpsiLog}{1 + logit(\q)}

\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[
  width=12.5cm, height=7.3cm,
  axis lines=left,
  xlabel={$z$}, ylabel={},
  xlabel style={at={(axis description cs:1,0)}, anchor=north west},
  xmin=-6, xmax=6,
  ymin=0, ymax=1.05,
  domain=-6:6,
  samples=400,
  clip=false,
  ticklabel style={font=\small},
  xtick=\empty,
  ytick=\empty]

% Baseline continuous CDF: Logistic centered at 1
\addplot[black, thin] {Logistic(x-1)};
\node[font=\Large] at (axis cs:2.2,{Logistic(1)-0.05}) {$\mathbb P$};

% Point mass at zstep: red thin line with vertical jump
\addplot[red, thin] coordinates {(-6,0) (\zstep,0)};
\addplot[red, thin] coordinates {(\zstep,0) (\zstep,1)};
\addplot[red, thin] coordinates {(\zstep,1) (6,1)};
\node[text=red, font=\Large] at (axis cs:1.8,1.05) {$\mathds{1}^*$};

% Label z*
\node[red, anchor=north] at (axis cs:\zstep,0) {$z^\ast$};

% Mixture CDF
\addplot[black!50!red, very thick]
  { (x<\zstep) * ((1-\eps)*Logistic(x-1)) + (x>=\zstep) * ((1-\eps)*Logistic(x-1) + \eps) };
\node[black!50!red, anchor=south west, font=\Large] at (axis cs:1.6,{Logistic(1)+0.1}) {$\mathbb P_\epsilon$};

% Horizontal line at y=q
\addplot[dotted, domain=-6:6] {\q};
\node[anchor=east] at (axis cs:-6,\q) {$q$};

% Intersection with mixture: psi_eps
\addplot[dotted] coordinates {(\xpsi,0) (\xpsi,\q)};
\node[black!50!red, anchor=north] at (axis cs:\xpsi,0) {$\psi_\epsilon$};

% Intersection with logistic-only: psi
\addplot[dotted] coordinates {(\xpsiLog,0) (\xpsiLog,\q)};
\node[anchor=north] at (axis cs:\xpsiLog,0) {$\psi$};

\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

CDFs along the convex path between some distribution $\p$ and the point mass $\mathbb 1^*$ at $z^*$.
:::

Let's find an explicit expression for $\psi_\eps = \Psi(\p_\eps)$. We'll break it down into two cases: $z^* \le \psi$ and $\psi < z^*$.

First, let's put the point mass $z^*$ to the left of the quantile $\psi = \Psi(\p)$, as is shown in @fig-quantile-gradient. For any value $z < z^*$ to the left of the point mass,

$$
\p^{(\eps)}(z) = \p(z)(1-\eps) \le \p(z) < \p(z^*) \le p(\psi) = q
$$

Therefore the smallest value $z$ for which $\p^{(\eps)}(z)$ is larger than $q$ must be *at or to the right* of $z^*$. In other words, the quantile at the perturbed distribution $\psi_\eps$ is larger than or equal to the location of the point mass $z^*$. This is also visible in @fig-quantile-gradient. Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Psi(\p_\eps) &= \inf \{ z: \p^{(\eps)}(z) \ge q \} \\
&= \inf \{ z: \p^{(\eps)}(z) \ge q, z^* \le z \} \\
&= \inf \{ z: (1-\eps)\p(z) + \eps 1(z^* \le z) \ge q, z^* \le z \} \\
&= \inf \{ z: (1-\eps)\p(z) + \eps  \ge q, z^* \le z \} \\
&= \max\bigg\{ \inf \{ z: (1-\eps)\p(z) + \eps  \ge q\},\ z^* \bigg\}\\
&= \max\left\{ \p^{-1}\left(\frac{q-\eps}{1-\eps}\right),\ z^* \right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality follows because $\p$ is continuous by assumption so the infimum $\ge q$ is attained at the above inverse.

Now we can take a pathwise derivative. By assumption $z^* < \psi = \p^{-1}(q) = \lim_{\eps \to 0} \p^{-1}\left(\frac{q-\eps}{1-\eps}\right)$. Therefore when $\eps$ is small enough, $\Psi(\p_\eps) = \p^{-1}\left(\frac{q-\eps}{1-\eps}\right)$ because this term is always larger than $z^*$ in the maximum above. By the chain rule,

$$
\ddeps \Psi(\p^{(\eps)}) = 
\left( \left. \frac{\dd \p^{-1}(z)}{\dd z} \right|_{z=q} \right)
\left( q - 1 \right)
= \frac{q-1}{p(q)}
$$

where $p$ is the density of $\p$. You should convince yourself that $\frac{\dd \p^{-1}(z)}{\dd z} = \frac{1}{p(z)}$.

Similar arguments to those above show that when the point mass is to the *right* of the quantile,

$$
\Psi(\p_\eps) = \min\left\{ \p^{-1}\left(\frac{q}{1-\eps}\right),\ z^* \right\},
$$

and the pathwise derivative is

$$
\ddeps \Psi(\p^{(\eps)}) = \frac{q}{p(q)}.
$$

Combining the two cases gives the gradient

$$
\grad\Psi(z) = \frac{q - 1(z \le \psi)}{p(\psi)}
$$
::::

Let's sum up everything we've learned about point mass contamination in one place:

:::: callout-note
# Point Mass Contamination

::: {#def-point-mass-contamination}
To derive the canonical gradient for an estimand $\Psi$ in a nonparametric model via point mass contamination, evaluate $$
\grad\Psi(z^*) = \ddeps \Psi\bigg(\p + \eps (\mathbb 1^*- \p) \bigg)
$$

where $\mathbb 1^*$ is a distribution that places all its probability mass at a point $z^*$. Usually this is easiest to do by temporarily assuming that the variables are all discrete.

If desired, then verify that $\dot\Psi_\p(s) = \p s \grad\Psi$ for all $s \in \eltwopz$. Convex paths usually suffice to compute the pathwise derivatives. If the check fails due to indicator functions on possibly continuous variables, it is likely the estimand is not pathwise differentiable in nonparametric models.
:::
::::

Point mass contamination is why influence functions are called influence functions. In the last chapter we proved that the efficient influence function $\phi^*$ is equal to the canonical gradient. So instead of writing the point mass contamination strategy with the gradient we can write it with the influence function

$$
\phi^*(z^*) = \ddeps \Psi(\p + \eps(\mathbb 1^* - \p).
$$

The pathwise derivative on the right-hand side measures the influence that an infinitesimally small point mass at $z^*$ exerts on the estimand (at $\p$). Thus the term "influence function". Another motivation for the term is that an asymptotically linear estimator is more sensitive to data points for which the value of the influence function is large. Because $\hat\Psi (\p_n) \approx \Psi(\p) + \frac{1}{n} \sum \phi^*(Z)$ in large samples, if we add a single data point $Z_{n+1}$ to a large-enough dataset, it will have the largest effect on the estimate if $\phi^*(Z_{n+1})$ is large. An estimator that has an influence function that takes many large values across its domain may be more sensitive to differences in datasets (e.g. outliers).

## Gradient Rules

Point mass contamination is a very useful strategy but the manual calculations required can quickly get out of hand for complex estimands. Even the algebra required to derive the gradient of the conditional mean in @exm-point-mass-cond-mean-EIF was a bit excessive. You can have a look at @hines-eif and @kennedy-review to review examples that are even more involved. Thankfully, the algebra can usually be simplified with the application of a few easy derivative rules.

To make an analogy to calculus, you probably don't remember how to derive the fact that the derivative of the log is the inverse function or that the derivative of sine is cosine, etc. Derivatives are tricky to compute from scratch! Nonetheless, you're probably pretty comfortable computing the derivative of $\sin(\log(x) + x^2)$ because you've memorized a few key primitive derivatives and you know how to use the chain, product, and sum rules. Deriving gradients is the same way: coming up with the primitives can be tricky, but once you have them it's usually just a matter of combining them in the right way to get gradients for more complex estimands.

:::: callout-note
# Gradient Rules

::: {#thm-gradient-rules}
Let $\Psi$ and $\Upsilon$ be two pathwise differentiable, scalar estimands defined on the same model and let $g: \reals \to \reals$ be a differentiable function and $c \in \reals$ some constant. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\grad(c \Psi + \Upsilon) &= c\grad\Psi + \grad \Upsilon \quad \text{(sum rule)} \\
\grad(\Psi \Upsilon) &= \Upsilon \grad\Psi + \Psi \grad \Upsilon \quad \text{(product rule)} \\
\grad g(\Psi) &= \grad_\Psi g\  \grad\Psi  \quad \text{(chain rule)}
.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
# Proof of Chain Rule

For any score $s \in \tspace$, $$
\dot{[g(\Psi)]}(s) \overset{\text{def}}= \ddeps g(\Psi(\p_\eps))
$$

where $\p_\eps$ is a differentiable path with score $s$. For any such path $\eps \mapsto \Psi(\p_\eps)$ maps reals to reals and moreover is differentiable because we assumed $\Psi$ was pathwise differentiable. Therefore, by the ordinary chain rule $\frac{\dd g(\psi(\eps))}{\dd \eps} = \frac{\dd g}{\dd \psi} \frac{\dd \psi}{\dd\eps}$,

$$
\ddeps g(\Psi(\p_\eps)) = 
\left( \left. \frac{\dd}{\dd \psi} \right|_{\psi = \Psi(\p)} g(\psi)\right)\ 
\underbrace{\left( \ddeps \Psi(\p_\eps) \right)}_{\dot\Psi(s)},
$$

meaning that $\dot{[g(\Psi)]} = \grad_\Psi g \ \dot\Psi$ where $\grad_\Psi g = \left. \frac{\dd}{\dd \psi} \right|_{\psi = \Psi(\p)} g(\psi)$ is just the usual derivative of $g$ evaluated at the point $\Psi(\p)$. Clearly $\dot{[g(\Psi)]}(s)$ exists and is bounded and linear since $\grad_\Psi g$ exists and is a constant and $\dot\Psi(s)$ exists and is bounded and linear. Therefore the estimand $g(\Psi)$ is pathwise differentiable.

The gradient of $g(\Psi)$ is the unique function $\grad g(\Phi)$ in the tangent space $\tspace$ that satisfies

$$
\dot{[g(\Psi)]}(s) = \p s \grad g(\Phi).
$$

But using our expression for the pathwise derivative $\dot{[g(\Psi)]}$ and the definition of the gradient of $\Psi$, we already know

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot{[g(\Psi)]}(s) 
&= \grad_\Psi g \ \dot\Psi(s) \\
&= \grad_\Psi g \p s\grad\Psi \\
&= \p s(\grad_\Psi g \grad\Psi),
\end{aligned}
$$

proving that $\grad_\Psi g \grad\Psi$ satisfies the condition required to be a gradient. Since $\grad\Psi \in \tspace$ and $\grad_\Psi g$ is a constant, this gradient is in the tangent space and is thus the canonical gradient.
:::

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-gradient-rules}
Using insights from the proof of the chain rule, prove the sum and product rules from @thm-gradient-rules.
:::
::::

These rules look exactly the same as the usual rules for derivatives because they follow from them. A gradient is simply a way of encoding the "slope" of a function in multiple dimensions.

The gradient rules make it easy to derive gradients for complicated estimands, including those relevant in causal inference.

::: {.Exm #exm-ATE-gradient}
# Gradient of the ATE in a nonparametric model

Let $\Psi$ be the observable average treatment effect $\Psi(\p) = \E_\p[\E_\p[Y|A=1,X] - \E_\p[Y|A=0,X]]$. To derive the nonparametric gradient we'll use a combination of gradient rules and point mass contamination. Abbreviate

$$
\mu(a,x) = \E_\p[Y|A=a,X=x]
$$

Notice that in a discrete model we can write

$$
\Psi = \underbrace{\sum_x \mu(1,x) \ p(x)}_{\Psi_1} - \underbrace{\sum_x \mu(0,x)\ p(x)}_{\Psi_0}  .
$$

We can treat the values $\mu(a,x)$ and $p(x)$ for all $a,x$ as their own estimands, and in fact we already know their gradients. Using the result from @exm-point-mass-cond-mean-EIF giving the gradient for a conditional mean at a point,

$$
\grad [\mu(\tilde a, \tilde x)] (y,a,x) = \frac{1_{(\tilde a, \tilde x)}(a,x)}{p(\tilde a, \tilde x)}
\big( y - \mu(\tilde a, \tilde x) \big).
$$

And, using the result from @exm-point-mass-density,

$$
\grad[ p(\tilde x)](x) = 1_{\tilde{x}}(x) - p(\tilde x).
$$

Now we combine these results using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\grad \Psi_{\tilde a} &= \grad\left[
    \sum_{\tilde{x}} \mu(\tilde a, \tilde x) \ p(\tilde x)
\right] 
\\
&= \sum_{\tilde{x}} \bigg( 
    \grad[\mu(\tilde a,\tilde x)]\ p(\tilde x) 
    + \mu(\tilde a,\tilde x) \ \grad[ p(\tilde x) ]
\bigg)
\\
&= \sum_{\tilde{x}} \left( 
    \frac{1_{(\tilde a, \tilde x)}(a,x)}{p(\tilde a, \tilde x)}
\big( y - \mu(\tilde a, \tilde x) \big) p(\tilde x) 
    + \mu(\tilde a,\tilde x) \big( 1_{\tilde{x}}(x) - p(\tilde x) \big)
\right)
\\
&= \frac{1_{\tilde{a}}(a)}{p(\tilde a |  x)}
\big( y - \mu(\tilde a,  x) \big) + \mu(\tilde a,  x) 
- \underbrace{\sum_{\tilde x} \mu(\tilde a, \tilde x) \ p(\tilde x)}_{\Psi_{\tilde{a}}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the tildes dropped off the $\tilde x$s after the last equality due to $1_{\tilde x}(x) = 1(\tilde x = x)$ picking out just the values corresponding to the value $x$ out of the sum. Finally, using the sum rule,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\grad \Psi 
&= \grad \Psi_1 - \grad \Psi_0 \\
&= \left(
    \frac{1_1(a)}{p(1 |  x)} \big( y - \mu(1,  x) \big) 
    + \mu(1,  x) - \Psi_1
\right)
-
\left(
    \frac{1_0(a)}{p(0 |  x)} \big( y - \mu(0,  x) \big) 
    + \mu(0,  x) - \Psi_0
\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

With a little bit of algebra, this can also be expressed as

$$
\grad\Psi(y,a,x) = \left(\frac{a}{p(1 |  x)} - \frac{1-a}{p(0 |  x)}\right) \big( y - \mu(a,  x) \big) 
    + \big[\mu(1,x) - \mu(0,  x)\big] - \Psi,
$$

which you may recognize if you've read any literature about doubly robust or efficient estimation of the average treatment effect.

In this example we used gradients of primitives like densities and conditional expectations at points that are not pathwise differentiable in general models. However, the ATE estimand *is* pathwise differentiable in general models. This is fairly typical: you can often use gradients from non-differentiable estimands and combine them to derive gradients for differentiable estimands.
:::

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-att-gradient}
# Gradient of the ATT

There are some cases in which the ATE cannot be identified, but the average effect on the *treated* (ATT) can. The ATT estimand is often identified by

$$
\Psi(\p) = \E_\p\left[\left(\E_\p[Y|A=1,X] - \E_\p[Y|A=0,X] \right) \big| A=1 \right].
$$

What is the canonical gradient for this estimand in a nonparametric model?

*Hint: assume a discrete model and decompose the estimand similarly to the ATE, then use your result from @exr-point-mass-conditional-density on the term* $p(x|A=1)$.
:::
::::

## Projection

Point mass contamination works for nonparametric models, but there are many interesting models that are restricted in some way for which we'd also like to derive the canonical gradient. In general, shrinking the model either reduces the tangent space or leaves it unchanged at each distribution, meaning that a function that was the canonical gradient in a larger model may not even be in the tangent space anymore.

However, we already showed that the nonparametric gradient is still *a* gradient of any restricted model. Let $\model \subset \mathcal Q$ be the restricted model inside of a larger (possibly locally nonparametric) model. The set of directions one can move in from any point $\p \in \model$ to stay within the model is a subset of the directions one can move in to stay within the larger model $\mathcal Q$. In other words, the tangent set in the smaller model is a subset of the tangent set in the larger model. A gradient of an estimand $\Psi$ in $\model$ is any function $\phi$ that satisfies $\dot\Psi_\p(s) = \p s\phi$ for all $s \in \tspace$. The canonical gradient in the larger model, which we will notate $\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}}_\p \Psi$, satisfies this for all the scores in the larger tangent space $\dot{\mathring Q}$, which includes the smaller tangent space $\tspace$.

Recall that any gradient relative to a tangent space $\tspace$ orthogonally decomposes into the sum of the canonical gradient relative to that tangent space and an element of its orthogonal complement. Therefore $\grad^\tspace_\p \Psi = \nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}}_\p \Psi + v$ where $v \in \tspace^\perp$. This is rephrased in the following theorem, which, in principle, gives us a way to derive an influence function for a smaller model if we know it in a larger model.

:::: callout-note
# Gradient Projection

::: {#thm-gradient-proj}
$\model \subseteq \mathcal Q$ be models and let $\Psi$ be an estimand that is pathwise differentiable at $\p$ in the larger model $\mathcal Q$ with canonical gradient $\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}}_\p \Psi$. The canonical gradient of $\Psi$ at $\p$ in the smaller model $\model$ is the orthogonal projection of the canonical gradient in the larger model onto the tangent space $\tspace$ of the smaller model:

$$
\grad^{\tspace}_\p \Psi = \tspace\left[ \nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}}_\p \Psi\right].
$$
:::
::::

::: {#fig-RAL-IF-set}

A visual representation of @thm-gradient-proj. The entirety of the depicted space is the tangent space $\mathring{\mathcal Q}$, with the tangent space $\tspace$ of the smaller model inside of it.
:::

@thm-gradient-proj illustrates why starting this chapter by discussing nonparametric models was a good idea: we often need the nonparametric gradient to derive the equivalent gradient in a restricted model. Admittedly, it's also possible to start with *any* gradient - the result of the theorem holds if $\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}}_\p \Psi$ is replaced with an arbitrary gradient of $\Psi$ in $\model$. But, in general, it's hard to know what is a gradient and what isn't: deriving the nonparametric canonical gradient is a surefire way to get a valid starting point.

To use theorem, assuming we have a nonparametric gradient already, we need to figure out the tangent space for the model of interest and derive a method for projecting onto it. Given our results from @thm-conditional-scores and @thm-factored-tset, both steps are easy for models where one or more factors of the distribution is restricted but others are left nonparametrically unspecified.

::: callout-warning
You may want to go back and re-read @sec-factoring before proceeding.
:::

:::: {.Exm #exm-ate-rct-gradient}
Let $(Y,A,X) \sim \p$ according to our standard outcome-treatment-covariate setup. Presume that we are working in a randomized trial so that our model $\model$ is distributions where we know $\p\{A=1|X\} = \frac{1}{2}$, but $\p\{Y|A,X\}$ and $\p\{X\}$ are allowed to be anything. Let's derive the canonical gradient of the average treatment effect within this randomized trial model by projecting the nonparametric canonical gradient onto the randomized trial tangent space.

The first step is to find the tangent space. Let $\mathcal Q$ be the fully nonparametric model where none of the factors are known so $\mathring{\mathcal Q} = \eltwopz$. As worked out in @exm-rct-tspace, the tangent space of this model is

$$
\tspace = \mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(X)} \oplus \mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(Y|A,X)},
$$

where, according to @thm-factored-tset,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(X)} &= \{s \in \eltwopz: s(y,a,x) = s(x) \} \\
\mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(Y|A,X)} &= \{s \in \eltwopz: \E[s(Y,A,X)|A,X] = 0\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The condition "$s(y,a,x) = s(x)$" is an abusive way of saying "all functions of $y,a,x$ that depend only on $x$".

Now we can figure out how to project onto this tangent space. Because the two components above are orthogonal subspaces, we may project a function onto each subspace and sum the results to obtain the projection onto $\tspace$:

$$
\tspace s = \mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(X)}s + \mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(Y|A,X)} s,
$$

as is illustrated in @fig-rct-gradient.

::: {#fig-rct-gradient}
``` tikz
\tdplotsetmaincoords{70}{120}

\def\RA{0.08} % right-angle marker leg length

% gradient tip coords in rotated plane
\pgfmathsetmacro{\gx}{0.8*\PlaneHalfX*cos(\GradAngle)}
\pgfmathsetmacro{\gy}{0.8*\PlaneHalfX*sin(\GradAngle)}
\pgfmathsetmacro{\PhiZ}{0.8*\NormalLen}
% gradient direction unit vector in plane coords
\pgfmathsetmacro{\ux}{cos(\GradAngle)}
\pgfmathsetmacro{\uy}{sin(\GradAngle)}

\resizebox{12cm}{!}{
\begin{tikzpicture}[tdplot_main_coords, scale=3.0, line cap=round, line join=round]

  \pgfmathsetmacro{\Lxy}{sqrt((\gx)^2+(\gy)^2)} % ||(gx,gy,0)||
  \pgfmathsetmacro{\ax}{\gx/\Lxy}                % unit along planar projection
  \pgfmathsetmacro{\ay}{\gy/\Lxy}

  \coordinate (CY) at ($(0,\gy,0) + (0,-\RA,0) + (\RA*\rxY,\RA*\ryY,\RA*\rzY)$);

  % From the corner, draw equal legs: +axis (toward projection) and -residual (toward projection)
  \draw[gray, very thin] (CX) -- ($ (CX) + (\RA,0,0) $);
  \draw[gray, very thin] (CX) -- ($ (CX) - (\RA*\rxX,\RA*\ryX,\RA*\rzX) $);

  \draw[gray, very thin] (CY) -- ($ (CY) + (0,\RA,0) $);
  \draw[gray, very thin] (CY) -- ($ (CY) - (\RA*\rxY,\RA*\ryY,\RA*\rzY) $);

\end{tikzpicture}
}
```

Visual illustration of the projection of the nonparametric gradient of the average treatment effect onto the tangent space for a randomized trial model. The projection is found by first projecting onto the two orthogonal subspaces of the tangent space and summing the results.
:::

The formulae from @thm-conditional-scores give us a way to do the projections:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left[\mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(X)} s\right] (x) &= \E[s(Y,A,X)|X=x] \\
\left[ \mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(Y|A,X)} s \right] (y,a,x) &= s(y,a,x) - \E[s(Y,A,X)|A=a,X=x]
.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-rct-projections}

In @exm-ATE-gradient, we derived that the canonical gradient of the ATE in the nonparametric model is the difference of the gradients of the treatment-specific means

$$
\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi = \nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_1 - \nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_0,
$$

where

$$
\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_a(Y,A,X) = \frac{1_a(A)}{\pi(a,X)} \big( Y - \mu(A, X) \big) 
    + \mu(a,X) - \Psi_a
$$

and $\pi(a,x) = \p\{A=a|X=x\}$ and $\mu(a,x) = \E_\p[Y|A=a,X=x]$. By the linearity of projection (@thm-orth-proj-linear), we may therefore project each of these components and sum the projections, i.e.,

$$
\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal P}} \Psi =
\tspace \left[\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi \right] = 
\tspace \left[ \nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_1 \right] - 
\tspace \left[ \nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_0 \right].
$$

Now we substitute $\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Phi_a$ for $s$ in @eq-rct-projections and compute the projections. We'll need the conditional expectation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E\left[\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_a(Y,A,X) \middle| A, X \right]
&= 
\E\left[ 
    \frac{1_a(A)}{\pi(a,X)} \big( Y - \mu(A, X) \big) 
    + \mu(a,X) - \Psi_a
\middle| A, X \right] \\
&=
\mu(a,X) - \Psi_a
.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-a-x-proj-ate}

We'll also need the equivalent conditional expectation conditioned just on $X$. But since $\E[f(Y,A,X)|X] = \E\big[\E[f(Y,A,X) |A,X] \big| X\big]$ by total expectation we can use the result above and save some work: $$
\begin{aligned}
\E\left[\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_a(Y,A,X) \middle| X \right]
&= 
\E\left[ 
   \mu(a,X) - \Psi_a
\middle| X \right] 
\\
&=
\mu(a,X) - \Psi_a
.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, plugging into @eq-rct-projections,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left[\mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(X)} \left(\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_a \right) \right] (x) &=  \mu(a,X) - \Psi_a \\
\left[ \mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(Y|A,X)} \left(\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_a \right)\right] (y,a,x) &=  \frac{1_a(A)}{\pi(a,X)} \big( Y - \mu(A, X) \big) 
,
\end{aligned}
$$

These are just the two terms of the nonparametric gradient for the treatment-specific mean. To get the projection onto the sum of these two subspaces, which is the randomized trial tangent space $\tspace$, we sum up the results:

$$
\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal P}} \Psi_a = \tspace \left(\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_a \right) = \nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi_a.
$$

Which of course implies the same for the gradient of the ATE, i.e. $\nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal P}} \Psi = \nabla^{\mathring{\mathcal Q}} \Psi$. This happens because the nonparametric gradient is already in the randomized trial tangent space: the projection does nothing to it.

The implication is that the canonical gradient for the average treatment effect is the *same* in a randomized trial model as it is in a nonparametric model. In turn, this means that the norm of the gradient is the same regardless and thus there is no gain in asymptotic efficiency in estimating the ATE in a randomized trial vs. in an observational study. If you are curious, @li2024efficient shows that even some strong restrictions on the outcome mechansim don't improve the efficiency bound! This is a remarkable fact that runs counter to our intuition: we typically expect that knowing more about the data-generating process should reduce our uncertainty. However, the example illustrates that there are some aspects of any data-generating process that are simply not relevant to particular estimands. To reduce uncertainty, the knowledge or assumptions must restrict the model in a way that is germane to the estimand. 

This example is the subject of @hahn1998role, a heavily-cited paper in the causal inference literature. The paper should not be interpreted to mean that there is no estimation benefit to having the true propensity score. Using the true propensity score when it is available is useful, as we will see in the next chapters. In a randomized trial, using an estimated rather than the known, true propensity score can increase the finite-sample variance of efficient estimates. There can be benefits to estimating the propensity score in a randomized trial if an *inefficient* estimator like IPW is used (see @exr-rct-ipw), but generally there is no point in doing that.
::::

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-rct-gradient-expectations}
Prove the equality in the second line of @eq-rct-projections using the definitions of $\mu(a,x)$ and $\pi(a,x)$. This is purely a refresher exercise in conditional expectation, no knowledge of efficiency theory is required.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-rct-ipw}
Althought the *canonical* gradient is the same whether or not the treatment mechanism is known, there is another difference between the randomized and observational settings that pertains to estimation. In @exr-ipw-irregular, you showed that the IPW estimator for the treatment-specific mean with fixed propensity model $\hat\pi(a,x)$ has influence function

$$
\phi(Y,A,X) = \frac{1_a(A)}{\hat\pi(a,X)}Y,
$$ {#eq-ipw-if}

which is not equal to the canonical gradient of the treatment-specific mean in a observational study. Because the model is nonparametric in that setting, the only influence function of a RAL estimator is the canonical gradient, which implies that the IPW estimator is not regular!

Is this the case in a randomized trial? When

$$
\tspace = \mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(X)} \oplus \mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(Y|A,X)},
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(X)} &= \{s \in \eltwopz: s(y,a,x) = s(x) \} \\
\mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(Y|A,X)} &= \{s \in \eltwopz: \E[s(Y,A,X)|A,X] = 0\},
\end{aligned}
$$

prove that the IPW influence function $\phi$ is a gradient of the treatment specific mean $\Psi_a(\p) = \E_\p[\E_\p[Y|A=a,X]]$ by showing that $\p s \phi = \p s \nabla^{\mathcal P}_\p \Psi$ for all $s \in \tspace$.

Since the set of gradients coincides with the set of influence functions of RAL estimators, your result shows that the fixed-propensity IPW estimator is a regular (but inefficient) estimator when the treatment mechanism is known.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-att-rct-gradient}
In our usual $(Y,A,X)$ data structure with $A$ binary, let

$$
\Psi(\p) = \E_\p\left[\left(\E_\p[Y|A=1,X] - \E_\p[Y|A=0,X] \right) \big| A=1 \right]
$$

be the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT). In @exr-att-gradient you should have derived that the nonparametric gradient of this estimand is

$$
\begin{split}
\grad\Psi(y,a,x)
= \frac{a}{\p\{A=1\}}
\left[(y-\mu(1,x))
  - \frac{1-a}{a}\frac{\pi(1,x)}{\pi(0,x)}(y-\mu(0,x))\right] \\
\qquad + \frac{a}{\p\{A=1\}}
\big[\mu(1,x) - \mu(0,x) - \psi\big].
\end{split}
$$

leaving off the $\p$ subscripts and letting $\psi = \Psi(\p)$, $\pi(a,x) = \p\{A=a|X=x\}$, and $\mu(a,x) = \E[Y|A=a,X=x]$ as usual.

Let $\mathcal P$ be the randomized trial model we considered in @exm-rct-tspace and @exm-ate-rct-gradient. What is the canonical gradient of the ATT in the randomized trial model? Given your conclusion, does treatment randomization result in a gain of estimation efficiency for the ATT or not? This question was also originally addressed by @hahn1998role.
:::
::::

The concept of having aspects of a data-generating distribution that are not relevant to a given estimand can be formalized. In @sec-classical-efficiency we introduced the idea of the nuisance tangent set. The idea is that this set contains all the directions through the model in which the distribution can be changed *without* affecting the value of the estimand. We can generalize the definition to nonparametric models: the *nuisance* tangent space of a pathwise differentiable estimand $\Psi$ at $\p$ is the smallest closed subspace of the tangent space contianing all scores for which $\dot\Psi_\p = 0$. If you remember linear algebra, you know this is the definition of the *null space* of $\dot\Psi_\p$, so we can also call it that. In a nonparametric model, the null space of the ATE's pathwise derivative includes $\mathring{\mathcal Q}^{(A|X)}$, which is why knowledge of the treatment mechanism has no effect on the optimal asymptotic variance when estimating the ATE.

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-rct-gradient-expectations}
Use @thm-RAL-IFs to prove that the null space of $\dot\Psi$ is also the orthogonal complement of the span of the canonical gradient, relative to the full tangent space.
:::
::::

At any $\p$, a model that is restricted only in the nusiance tangent space of an estimand will not affect the value of the canonical gradient of that estimand relative to the nonparametric model. The reason is simple: restricting the way a distribution can vary that doesn't affect the estimand has no effect on how hard it is to estimate that estimand.

The concept of a nuisance tangent space is also relevant in other restricted models. I give the theorem and example below not because they have much practical utility, but because understanding the result is a good summative exercise of all the tools we've learned relating to gradients and tangent spaces. And also it's just plain cool.

:::: callout-note
# Estimand-Restricted Models
::: {#thm-estimand-restricted-models}
Let $\Psi$ and $\Upsilon$ be two estimands that are pathwise differentiable at $\p$ in some model $\mathcal Q$. Let $\model = \{\p \in \mathcal Q: \Upsilon(\p) = \upsilon\}$ be all distributions where $\Psi$ is fixed at the value $\upsilon \in \reals$ and let $\{\nabla_\p^{\mathcal Q} \Upsilon \} = \{c \nabla_\p^{\mathcal Q} \Upsilon: c \in \reals\}$ be the span of the gradient of $\Psi$ in $\mathcal Q$. Then 

$$
\tspace_\p = \{\nabla_\p^{\mathcal Q} \Upsilon \}^\perp
$$

where the orthogonal complement is relative to the tangent space $\mathring{\mathcal Q}$ in the unrestricted model. As a consequence of the gradient projection theorem (@thm-gradient-proj) and the one-dimensional projection formula (@thm-1d-proj), 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\p^{\mathcal P} \Psi
&= \tspace_\p (\nabla_\p^{\mathcal Q} \Psi) \\
&= \nabla_\p^{\mathcal Q} \Psi -  \frac{\left\langle \nabla_\p^{\mathcal Q} \Upsilon, \nabla_\p^{\mathcal Q} \Psi \right\rangle}{\|\nabla_\p^{\mathcal Q} \Upsilon\|^2} \nabla_\p^{\mathcal Q} \Upsilon.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

The theorem seems complicated but it actually follows immediately from the definitions. When the estimand $\Upsilon$ is fixed, the only directions that distributions in the restricted model $\model$ are allowed to vary in are precisely those in which $\Upsilon$ doesn't change, i.e., $s$ where $\dot\Upsilon(s) = 0$. Therefore that is the tangent set of the model. By the central identity, the scores that satisfy $0 = \dot\Upsilon_\p (s) = \p s \grad\Upsilon$ are those orthogonal to the gradient. The rest is the one-dimensional projection formula.

::: {.Exm #exm-estimand-restricted-model}
Let's say you know for a fact that the median of a random variable $Z$ is $\upsilon$, but are interested in estimating the mean from a sample of data. This isn't a scenario you're likely to encounter, but to make things concrete you might imagine that the median age in a population is reported as a summary of a population census, but the mean age isn't. You don't have access to the original census dataset, but you do have access to a much smaller sample. You want to estimate the mean age from that smaller sample, but want to know if incorporating prior knowledge of the median can yield any gain in certainty. 

Let $\Psi$ map a one-dimensional continuous distribution to its mean and let $\Upsilon$ map to its median. In @exm-gradient-nonparam and @exm-quantile-gradient we established that the nonparametric gradients of these estimands are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\grad\Psi(z) &= z - \psi \\
\grad\Upsilon &= \frac{q - 1(z\ge \upsilon)}{p(q)} 
\end{aligned} 
$$

where I've omitted the $\p$ subscripts and abbreviated $\psi = \Psi(\p)$, $\upsilon = \Upsilon(\p)$, and $q=1/2$. As usual, $p$ is the density of $\p$. 

By @thm-estimand-restricted-models, the canonical gradient of the mean in the model where the median is known must be

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla^{\mathcal P} \Psi
&= \grad \Psi -  \frac{\left\langle \grad \Upsilon, \grad \Psi \right\rangle}{\|\grad \Upsilon\|^2} \grad \Upsilon.
\end{aligned}
$$

The inner product and norm are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\langle \grad \Upsilon, \grad \Psi \right\rangle 
&= \E\left[ (z - \psi) \left( \frac{q - 1(z\ge \upsilon)}{p(q)}  \right) \right] \\
&= \frac{q(\psi - \E[Z | Z \ge \upsilon])}{p(q)} \\
\|\grad \Upsilon\|^2 
&= \E \left[ \frac{(q - 1(z\ge \upsilon))^2}{p(q)^2} \right] \\
&= \frac{q(1-q)}{p(q)^2}
\end{aligned}
$$

since, by definition, $q = \p\{Z \ge \upsilon\} = \E[1(Z \ge \upsilon)]$. Combining,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla^{\mathcal P} \Psi(z)
&= (z-\psi) 
-  \frac{\psi - \E[Z | Z \ge \upsilon]}{1-q} (q - 1(z\ge \upsilon)).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is generally different than the nonparametric gradient $\grad \Psi$, the projection must have reduced the norm of the gradient and therefore improved the asymptotic efficiency. Knowing the median therefore theoretically improves our ability to estimate the mean, which is intuitively plausible.

:::
